full_title: NATIONAL BUREAU OF INVESTIGATION, REGION VII, PETITIONER, VS. AVELINO J. GUNGOB, SR., RESPONDENT.
subject: Political and Public International Law
syllabus_topic: XI. Law on Public Officers > D. Accountability of Public Officers (RA 6713) > 2. Discipline > a. Grounds
topics: Good faith is not a defense to simple misconduct
Mayor's extraction of minerals without a permit (Sec. 103, RA 7942)
Service on counsel: notice to the party is not notice in law (Rule 13, Sec. 2)
Reglementary period runs from the OSG's receipt

other_subjects.subject: Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics
other_subjects.syllabus_topic: III. Civil Procedure > E. Pleadings > 10. Filing and Service (Rules 13 and 13-A, as amended; AM 10-3-7-SC, 11-9-4-SC, 25-01-13-SC, and 25-09-16-SC)

doctrine:
**Misconduct is a transgression of an established and definite rule of action, more particularly unlawful behavior or gross negligence by a public officer. It is grave only if it involves corruption, willful intent to violate the law, or disregard of established rules, proved by substantial evidence; otherwise it is simple** (*CSC v. Ledesma*). A person charged with grave misconduct may be held liable for simple misconduct. Plain unlawful behavior by a public officer, even without bad faith, malice or corrupt motive, already constitutes simple misconduct, because **good faith is not a defense to simple misconduct** (*Faeldonea v. CSC*). A mayor who directed the extraction and hauling of limestone without the required permits, a prima facie violation of Section 103 of the Philippine Mining Act (RA 7942), is liable for simple misconduct. It does not matter that the materials were used for bona fide municipal projects or that he had repeatedly asked the province to renew the municipality's gratuitous permit.

**When a party is represented by counsel, judgments and other papers must be served on counsel (Rule 13, Sec. 2, 1997 and 2019 Rules). Notice to the party itself is not notice in law and does not start the reglementary period.** A government agency represented by the OSG has 15 days from the OSG's receipt of the decision, not from the agency's own earlier receipt, to move for reconsideration. Reiterated (*Soriano v. Soriano*; *Villalongha v. CA*).
facts:
On November 26, 2009, the NBI Central Visayas office, together with a lawyer of the Provincial Treasurer's Office, the Cebu Provincial Police Office and Army soldiers, set up checkpoints in Barangays Danglag, Garing and Dagongdong, Consolacion, Cebu to stop illegal extraction and hauling of minerals. They apprehended three ten-wheeler dump trucks loaded with limestone or diorite used as filling material, and seized a backhoe and a bulldozer at the quarry site. All belonged to the Municipality of Consolacion, whose mayor was respondent Avelino Gungob, Sr.

On December 3, 2009, NBI Region VII filed a complaint before the Office of the Ombudsman against Gungob and seven job-order employees (the drivers and operators) for theft of minerals under Section 103 of RA 7942. Gungob explained that the materials were excavated for the municipality's "Mountain Highway Project," whose Environmental Compliance Certificate required their prompt removal, and were used as fill for a new transport terminal and the "Government Center Project." The province had granted the municipality a gratuitous permit on April 29, 2008, which expired when the terminal was completed. The province did not act on the municipality's application for a new permit despite follow-ups. To avoid delaying the projects, the hauling continued until the apprehension.

In a Joint Resolution dated February 9, 2015, the Ombudsman found probable cause for theft of minerals under Section 103, in relation to Section 49, of RA 7942. In the administrative case, it found Gungob guilty of simple misconduct and suspended him without pay for three months, convertible into a fine equal to three months' salary if he had left the service. Reconsideration was denied on April 23, 2015.

On Gungob's petition for review, the CA (March 13, 2019) ruled that it had no jurisdiction over the criminal aspect. It exonerated Gungob administratively: he acted in utmost good faith to implement bona fide municipal projects and had written the governor at least five times between January and October 2009 for renewal of the permit. The NBI received the CA decision on March 29, 2019, and the OSG, its counsel, received it on April 4, 2019. The OSG moved for reconsideration on April 16, 2019. The CA denied the motion as one day late, counting from the NBI's receipt (October 2, 2019 Resolution). The NBI filed a Rule 45 petition.
issues: Whether the CA erred in denying the NBI's motion for reconsideration as filed out of time, by counting the period from the NBI's receipt of the decision instead of the OSG's.
Whether the respondent mayor is administratively liable for simple misconduct despite his good faith.
ruling:
**1. Yes, the CA erred.** Under Rule 13, Section 2 of the 1997 Rules, substantially carried over in the 2019 Rules, service on a party who has appeared by counsel must be made on counsel unless the court orders otherwise. Service on anyone other than the counsel of record "is not legally effective and binding upon the party, nor may it start the corresponding reglementary period" (*Soriano v. Soriano*). The reason is that parties generally do not know the rules of procedure, and courts should deal with only one person in the interest of orderly procedure (*Villalongha v. CA*). The NBI was represented by the OSG, which prepared and filed the motion. **The period ran from the OSG's receipt on April 4, 2019, so the motion was due on April 19, 2019.** The motion filed on April 16, 2019 was timely.

**2. Yes, the mayor is guilty of simple misconduct.** The Ombudsman was correct. It was undisputed that the mayor directed the extraction and transport of earth materials and limestone without the necessary government permits. That act is a prima facie violation of Section 103 of RA 7942, which punishes extracting and disposing of minerals without a mining agreement, lease, permit or license. The CA erred in exonerating him because of good faith: "Good faith is not anathema to a finding of liability for simple misconduct." In *Faeldonea v. CSC*, a postmaster's good intentions negated grave misconduct but did not excuse him from simple misconduct. Like that postmaster, the mayor "ought to remain administratively accountable for his transgression of the law despite his good faith." The Ombudsman's administrative ruling was reinstated.
disposition: The Petition was GRANTED. The CA's March 13, 2019 Decision and October 2, 2019 Resolution in CA-G.R. SP No. 09439 were REVERSED and SET ASIDE. Gungob was found GUILTY of SIMPLE MISCONDUCT and SUSPENDED WITHOUT PAY for three months, with the accessory penalties. If the suspension can no longer be enforced because he has left the service, it is converted into a FINE equal to three months' salary, which may be deducted from his retirement benefits, accrued leave credits or other receivables from his office.

bar_questions.q: Mayor Delfin ordered municipal dump trucks to haul limestone from a municipal road project to fill the site of a new public market. The municipality's gratuitous permit to extract and haul the limestone had expired, and the provincial governor ignored Delfin's five written requests for its renewal. Delfin acted only to avoid delaying the projects and gained nothing personally. The Ombudsman found him guilty of simple misconduct. The Court of Appeals reversed, holding that his good faith negates any misconduct. Is the CA correct?

alac.answer: No. Delfin is liable for simple misconduct despite his good faith.
alac.legal_basis: Misconduct is a transgression of an established and definite rule of action, more particularly unlawful behavior or gross negligence by a public officer. It is grave only if attended by corruption, willful intent to violate the law, or disregard of established rules; otherwise it is simple. Plain unlawful behavior, even without bad faith, malice or corrupt motive, is simple misconduct, and good faith is not a defense to it. Extracting and disposing of minerals without a permit is punished under Section 103 of RA 7942. (NBI v. Gungob, G.R. No. 249916, August 13, 2025, citing CSC v. Ledesma and Faeldonea v. CSC)
alac.application: Delfin directed the extraction and hauling of limestone without a valid permit, which is a prima facie violation of Section 103 of RA 7942 and therefore unlawful behavior. His good faith, his public purpose and the governor's inaction may show that there was no corruption or willful intent, so his misconduct is not grave. But they do not erase the transgression itself.
alac.conclusion: The CA erred; Delfin should be held liable for simple misconduct.

bar_questions.q: Suppose the Ombudsman had charged Mayor Delfin with grave misconduct for the same hauling. (a) If the evidence shows no corruption and no willful intent to violate the law, but only that he hauled limestone without a permit in good faith, may he be held liable for simple misconduct under a charge of grave misconduct? (b) If the evidence instead shows by substantial evidence that he sold the limestone to a private contractor and kept the proceeds, what offense did he commit?

alac.answer: (a) Yes. He may be held liable for simple misconduct. (b) Grave misconduct, because the element of corruption is present.
alac.legal_basis: Misconduct becomes grave only if it involves any of the additional elements of corruption, willful intent to violate the law, or disregard of established rules, which must be established by substantial evidence; otherwise it is simple. A person charged with grave misconduct may be held liable for simple misconduct if the misconduct lacks the elements that qualify it as grave. (NBI v. Gungob, G.R. No. 249916, August 13, 2025, quoting CSC v. Ledesma)
alac.application: (a) Hauling without a permit is unlawful behavior. Without proof of corruption or willful intent, the qualifying elements are missing, so he may be found guilty of the lesser offense of simple misconduct. (b) Selling public minerals to a private party and pocketing the proceeds shows corruption, an additional element that makes the misconduct grave.
alac.conclusion: Without the qualifying elements, Delfin is liable only for simple misconduct; if corruption is proved by substantial evidence, he is liable for grave misconduct.

bar_questions.q: In an administrative appeal, the Court of Appeals decided against a government bureau, which is represented by the Office of the Solicitor General. The bureau's regional office received a copy of the decision on June 3. The OSG, its counsel of record, received its copy on June 10. The OSG filed a motion for reconsideration on June 24. The CA denied the motion as late, counting 15 days from June 3. Is the CA correct?

alac.answer: No. The motion was filed on time.
alac.legal_basis: Under Rule 13, Section 2 of the Rules of Court, when a party has appeared by counsel, service must be made on counsel. Notice to the party itself is not notice in law and does not start the reglementary period for the next procedural step. The 15-day period to move for reconsideration therefore runs from counsel's receipt. (NBI v. Gungob, G.R. No. 249916, August 13, 2025)
alac.application: The bureau is represented by the OSG, so only the OSG's receipt on June 10 counts. Fifteen days from June 10 is June 25. The motion filed on June 24 was within the period. The bureau's own receipt on June 3 is not notice in law.
alac.conclusion: The CA erred in denying the motion as late; it was timely filed.

notes: First Division. Gesmundo, C.J. (Chairperson), Hernando, Zalameda and Marquez, JJ. concurred. The CA ruled that it had no jurisdiction over the criminal aspect (the Ombudsman's finding of probable cause for theft of minerals under Section 103, in relation to Section 49, of RA 7942); only the administrative aspect reached the Court. The decision does not discuss whether the complainant NBI had standing to appeal the exoneration. It calls the CA petition simply a "Petition for Review."
